rows.stem: Which of the following belongs to the class of Vinyl halides ?
rows.solution:
The vinyl halide is \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}C(Br){-}CH_3}\).

A VINYL (or vinylic) halide has its halogen attached DIRECTLY to a carbon that is part of a CARBON-CARBON DOUBLE BOND — an \(sp^2\) carbon. Here the bromine sits on the middle carbon, which is doubly bonded to the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), so it qualifies.

The other three fail on where the halogen sits. In \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}CH_2{-}Br}\) the halogen is on the \(sp^3\) carbon NEXT TO the double bond — that is an ALLYLIC halide, a quite different and far more reactive class. In \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCH_2CH_2Cl}\) it is further away still. And in \(\mathrm{CH{\equiv}C{-}Br}\) the carbon is \(sp\), part of a TRIPLE bond, which makes it an alkynyl halide.

The distinction matters chemically: a vinyl halide is exceptionally UNREACTIVE towards substitution, an allylic halide exceptionally reactive.

rows.stem: What is the secondary valency of Cobalt in \(\mathrm{[Co(en_2)Cl_2]^+}\) ?
rows.solution:
The secondary valency is SIX.

Secondary valency is Werner's term for the COORDINATION NUMBER — the count of DONOR ATOMS bonded directly to the metal.

Count them here. Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE, binding through both of its nitrogens, so two of them supply \(2 \times 2 = 4\) donor atoms; the two chlorido ligands supply one each. That gives
\(4 + 2 = 6\)
and the complex is octahedral.

Counting four LIGANDS instead of six donor atoms gives 4, which is the answer the question is testing for. The PRIMARY valency here is 3, matching cobalt's \(+3\) oxidation state — two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) against an ion of \(+1\).

rows.stem: When Benzene diazonium chloride reacts with phenol, it forms a dye. This reaction is called
rows.solution:
The reaction is a COUPLING REACTION.

A diazonium salt is a weak ELECTROPHILE, and it can attack only a very strongly activated ring. Phenol qualifies — in the mildly alkaline medium used it is present as the still more activated PHENOXIDE ion — so the diazonium ion attacks it at the PARA position:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}N{=}N{-}C_6H_4{-}OH} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The product is p-hydroxyazobenzene, an ORANGE dye. The intense colour comes from the extended conjugation running through the \(-\mathrm{N{=}N}-\) bridge and both rings.

DIAZOTISATION is the step BEFORE this one, making the diazonium salt from the amine. Aniline couples in the same way, giving p-aminoazobenzene.

rows.stem: The slope in the plot of \([\mathrm{R}]\) vs. time for a zero order reaction is
rows.solution:
The slope is \(-k\).

A zero order reaction proceeds at a constant rate, \(\text{Rate} = k\), so integrating gives
\([\mathrm{R}] = [\mathrm{R}]_0 - kt\)

Compare with \(y = c + mx\), taking \(y\) as \([\mathrm{R}]\) and \(x\) as \(t\): the intercept is the starting concentration and the slope is \(-k\).

The slope is NEGATIVE because the reactant is being consumed, and the line is STRAIGHT all the way to zero — which is the signature of zero order, since every other order gives a curve on these axes.

The two options carrying 2.303 belong to the FIRST order plot of \(\log[\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\), where the slope is \(-k/2{\cdot}303\).

Proteins are polymers of AMINO ACIDS.

Specifically of \(\alpha\)-amino acids, joined by PEPTIDE LINKAGES: the carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is lost, and the bond \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\) results.

About twenty different amino acids build all the proteins in the body, and the SEQUENCE in which they are arranged is the protein's primary structure — the level from which all the higher folding follows.

The other options name the monomers of other biopolymers. Nucleotides, not nucleic acids, build DNA and RNA; monosaccharides build polysaccharides such as starch and cellulose; amines are not polymerised biologically in this way at all.

rows.stem: Retention of configuration is observed in
rows.solution:
The scheme keys RETENTION to the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction.

The reasoning is by elimination. An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction gives INVERSION and nothing else: the nucleophile attacks from the side directly opposite the leaving group, in a single step, so every product molecule has had its configuration turned inside out. Retention is impossible there.

An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction goes through a PLANAR carbocation, which the nucleophile can attack from EITHER face. Attack on the face the leaving group vacated gives RETENTION; attack on the other face gives inversion. Roughly equal amounts of each are formed, so the product is racemic — but half of it does retain the original configuration, and it is the only one of the two mechanisms in which any retained product appears at all.

So the two mechanisms are distinguished exactly by this: \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) gives pure inversion, \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) gives both.

rows.stem: An azeotropic mixture of two liquids will have a boiling point lower than either of the two liquids when it

options.label: A
options.text: shows a negative deviation from Raoult's law

options.label: C
options.text: shows a positive deviation from Raoult's law

rows.solution:
An azeotrope boiling lower than either component shows a POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

A positive deviation means the observed vapour pressure is HIGHER than predicted, because the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are weaker than those between like ones, so the molecules escape more readily.

Higher vapour pressure means a LOWER boiling point — the mixture reaches atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature — so the azeotrope is a MINIMUM BOILING one. Ethanol with water is the familiar case, boiling at 351.1 K against water's 373 K, which is why absolute alcohol cannot be obtained by simple distillation.

A NEGATIVE deviation does the reverse and gives a maximum boiling azeotrope; an ideal solution forms no azeotrope at all.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the following does not give Cannizaro reaction ?
rows.solution:
The one that does NOT give the Cannizzaro reaction is \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CH{-}CHO}\), 2-methylpropanal.

Cannizzaro is the disproportionation of an aldehyde that has NO \(\alpha\)-HYDROGEN — one with an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen undergoes the ALDOL reaction instead, which is the easier route.

Check the carbon next to each carbonyl. In 2-methylpropanal that carbon carries a HYDROGEN, so the aldol route is open and Cannizzaro does not occur.

The other three have none. \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CHO}\) has its neighbouring carbon fully substituted by three methyls; \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\) has a benzene ring there; and \(\mathrm{HCHO}\) has no neighbouring carbon at all, only hydrogens on the carbonyl itself.

The presence or absence of a single \(\alpha\)-hydrogen therefore decides which of two quite different reactions an aldehyde undergoes.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydroxylamine to form
rows.solution:
Aldehydes and ketones react with hydroxylamine to form an OXIME.

Hydroxylamine, \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}OH}\), is an ammonia derivative: its nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon, water is lost, and a carbon-nitrogen double bond forms:
\(\mathrm{R_2C{=}O} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R_2C{=}N{-}OH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The other options are the products of the neighbouring ammonia derivatives, and the pattern is worth holding together. HYDRAZINE, \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}NH_2}\), gives a HYDRAZONE. SEMICARBAZIDE, \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}NH{-}CONH_2}\), gives a SEMICARBAZONE. And a CYANOHYDRIN comes from hydrogen cyanide, which is an addition rather than a condensation — no water is lost.

All of these condensations are reversible and acid-catalysed, and the crystalline products with their sharp melting points are used to identify the parent carbonyl compound.

rows.stem: For a reaction \(2\mathrm{A} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{B}\), rate of reaction \(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is equal to
rows.solution:
For \(2\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow 3\mathrm{B}\),
\(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Build it from the stoichiometry. Each species is divided by its coefficient, the reactant taking a minus sign because it is being consumed:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Multiplying through by 2 to isolate the term asked for:
\(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

The physical content is that \(\mathrm{B}\) appears FASTER than \(\mathrm{A}\) disappears — three produced for every two consumed — so the fraction multiplying the \(\mathrm{B}\) term must be less than 1. The option with \(3/2\) has the ratio inverted.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which one among the following metals of 3d series has the lowest melting point ?
rows.solution:
ZINC has the lowest melting point of the four, and indeed of the whole 3d series.

Melting a metal means overcoming its metallic bonding, and in a transition metal that bonding draws on the \((n-1)d\) electrons as well as the \(ns\) electrons — the more UNPAIRED d electrons available, the stronger it is.

Zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\): its d subshell is COMPLETELY FILLED, so those electrons are all paired and take no part in the bonding. Only the two \(4s\) electrons do, the interatomic forces are correspondingly weak, and zinc melts at just 693 K.

The others all have unpaired d electrons contributing: manganese melts at about 1518 K, copper at 1358 K, iron at 1808 K. The same fact explains zinc's softness and its low enthalpy of atomisation.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Elevation in boiling point is a colligative property.
Reason (R) : The lowering of vapour pressure of solution causes elevation in boiling point.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Elevation of boiling point IS a colligative property, and the lowering of vapour pressure IS what causes it — both statements hold.

But the second does not explain the first. The Reason gives the MECHANISM by which the boiling point rises: a non-volatile solute lowers the solvent's vapour pressure, so the solution must be heated further before its vapour pressure matches the atmospheric pressure.

What makes the effect COLLIGATIVE is something else — that the size of the lowering depends on the NUMBER of solute particles and not on their nature. The Reason explains why there is an elevation at all; it does not explain why the elevation is colligative.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Chlorobenzene is resistant to electrophilic substitution reaction.
Reason (R) : C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene acquires partial double bond characters due to resonance.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Chlorobenzene is indeed less reactive than benzene towards electrophilic substitution, and the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond does acquire partial double bond character from resonance — both statements are correct.

But they explain DIFFERENT things. Partial double bond character concerns the strength of the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond, and it is the reason chlorobenzene resists NUCLEOPHILIC substitution — the bond will not break.

Resistance to ELECTROPHILIC substitution has a different cause: chlorine's strong \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect WITHDRAWS electron density from the whole ring, so the ring is poorer at attacking an electrophile than benzene's is. Chlorine is DEACTIVATING.

The two properties are often stated side by side and are easy to attach to the wrong mechanism, which is exactly what this question is testing.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Transition metals have high enthalpy of atomisation.
Reason (R) : Greater number of unpaired electrons in transition metals results in weak metallic bonding.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Transition metals do have high enthalpies of atomisation — chromium's is about 397 kJ per mole against sodium's 108.

But the Reason reverses the effect. A greater number of unpaired electrons results in STRONG metallic bonding, not weak. Those unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons take part in the bonding alongside the \(ns\) electrons, and the more of them there are, the stronger the interatomic interaction.

And that is exactly why the Assertion holds: enthalpy of atomisation measures the energy needed to overcome precisely that bonding. The Reason, corrected, would have explained the Assertion; as written it would predict the opposite.

ZINC is the case that proves it, with a full d subshell, no unpaired d electrons, and the lowest enthalpy of atomisation in the series.

rows.stem:
(a) What is the difference between a nucleoside and nucleotide ?
(b) What products would be formed when a nucleotide from DNA containing thymine is hydrolysed ?
rows.solution:
(a) The difference is ONE COMPONENT — the phosphate.

A NUCLEOSIDE has TWO parts: a NITROGENOUS BASE joined to a PENTOSE SUGAR, the base attaching at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) of the sugar.

A NUCLEOTIDE has THREE: the same base and sugar, PLUS a PHOSPHATE GROUP esterifying the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_5}\).

The phosphate is what makes the chain possible — it links the \(\mathrm{C_5}\) of one sugar to the \(\mathrm{C_3}\) of the next, building the backbone of a nucleic acid. A nucleoside alone cannot do that.

(b) Hydrolysing a nucleotide breaks it into its three components:
THYMINE (the base), \(\beta\)-D-2-DEOXYRIBOSE (the sugar) and PHOSPHORIC ACID.

Note that the sugar is the DEOXY one, since the nucleotide comes from DNA; an RNA nucleotide would give ribose, and its fourth base would be uracil rather than thymine.

rows.stem:
Write the chemical equation involved in the following :
(a) Kolbe's reaction
(b) Williamson synthesis
rows.solution:
(a) KOLBE'S REACTION. Phenol is first converted to sodium PHENOXIDE, which is more strongly activated than phenol itself and nucleophilic enough to attack even a feeble electrophile. It attacks CARBON DIOXIDE at its ORTHO position, and acidification then frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CO_2}} \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}COOH}\)

The product is SALICYLIC ACID — the starting material for aspirin.

(b) WILLIAMSON SYNTHESIS. A sodium alkoxide displaces halide from an alkyl halide in a single bimolecular step:
\(\mathrm{R{-}O^-Na^+} + \mathrm{R'{-}X} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'} + \mathrm{NaX}\)

Because the step is \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), the HALIDE must be primary; a tertiary halide has too crowded a carbon and the alkoxide — a strong base as well as a nucleophile — eliminates instead, giving an alkene.

Its value is that it makes UNSYMMETRICAL ethers, which dehydrating an alcohol cannot.
